propositions.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of two decisions: an exclusion order and an appeal dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Dorinela Pepa, seeks judicial review of two (2) decisions. In IMM-6268-19, she challenges the exclusion order issued against her by the Immigration Division [ID] on October 16, 2018 [Exclusion Order], because of misrepresentation in acquiring permanent resident status in Canada. In IMM-6270-19, she challenges the Immigration Appeal Division [IAD]’s decision, dated August 27, 2019, dismissing her appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant seeks judicial review of two decisions: an exclusion order and an appeal dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.

propositions.text: The applications for judicial review are dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the applications for judicial review are dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the applications for judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a 23-year-old Albanian citizen who received a permanent resident visa on February 4, 2018.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 23-year-old citizen of Albania. On February 4, 2018, she was issued a permanent resident visa as an accompanying dependant of her father, who in turn was being sponsored to Canada by his new wife.

propositions.text: The Applicant’s visa was valid until September 16, 2018.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s visa was valid until September 16, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a 23-year-old Albanian citizen with a permanent resident visa valid until September 16, 2018.

propositions.text: The Applicant married on February 27, 2018, but did not inform immigration authorities.
propositions.quote: On February 27, 2018, the Applicant married. She did not advise immigration authorities of her marriage.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant married on February 27, 2018, without informing immigration authorities.

propositions.text: The Applicant arrived in Canada on March 20, 2018, and disclosed her marriage to the port of entry officer.
propositions.quote: On March 20, 2018, the Applicant arrived in Canada to become a permanent resident. Upon initial examination, she advised the port of entry officer that she was now married.

propositions.text: Due to the change in status, the Applicant was admitted for further examination rather than landed immediately.
propositions.quote: As a result of the change in status, the Applicant was not landed in Canada, but was rather admitted for further examination.

propositions.text: The examinations were completed on April 6, 2018.
propositions.quote: The examinations were completed on April 6, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant arrived March 20, 2018, disclosed marriage, was admitted for further examination, completed April 6, 2018.

propositions.text: At examination, the Applicant said she filed for divorce on March 29, 2018.
propositions.quote: When she attended the examination, the Applicant informed the officer that she filed for divorce on March 29, 2018.

propositions.text: On April 6, 2018, an officer prepared a subsection 44(1) report alleging inadmissibility under paragraph 41(a) of IRPA for failing to comply with paragraph 51(b) of the Regulations.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding, on April 6, 2018, the officer prepared a report under subsection 44(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], alleging that the Applicant was inadmissible under paragraph 41(a) of the IRPA for failing to comply with the requirements found in paragraph 51(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [Regulations].

propositions.text: The Minister’s Delegate referred the report to the Immigration Division for an admissibility hearing the next day.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s Delegate referred the report to the ID for an admissibility hearing the next day.

propositions.text: The Applicant’s visa was not cancelled at that time.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s visa was not cancelled.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant said she filed for divorce; an April 6 report alleged inadmissibility; referral to ID; visa not cancelled.

propositions.text: A further subsection 44(1) report was issued July 13, 2018, based on paragraph 40(1)(a) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: A further subsection 44(1) report was issued on July 13, 2018, based on paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The officer believed the Applicant’s failure to inform immigration officials of her marital status change induced an error in IRPA administration.
propositions.quote: In the officer’s view, the Applicant’s failure to inform the Canadian immigration officials responsible for processing her application for permanent residence of her change in marital status prior to her arrival in Canada induced an error in the administration of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The Applicant’s visa remained valid after this report.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s visa remained valid.

propositions.text: This report led to a further referral under subsection 44(2) of IRPA dated July 24, 2018.
propositions.quote: This report led to a further referral under subsection 44(2) of the IRPA, dated July 24, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a July 13 report alleged misrepresentation; visa remained valid; led to further referral July 24, 2018.

propositions.text: An admissibility hearing before the Immigration Division began September 25, 2018.
propositions.quote: An admissibility hearing before the ID commenced on September 25, 2018.

propositions.text: The Respondent abandoned the April report and proceeded only on the July report grounds of misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: At the outset of the hearing, the Respondent advised that it was abandoning the April subsection 44(1) report relating to inadmissibility under paragraph 41(a) of the IRPA and would proceed only on the grounds of the subsection 44(1) July report relating to misrepresentation.

propositions.text: The Immigration Division received evidence and submissions from both parties.
propositions.quote: The ID received evidence and submissions from both the Applicant and the Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the admissibility hearing started September 25, 2018; Respondent abandoned April report; evidence received from both parties.

propositions.text: After the hearing, Applicant’s counsel raised procedural fairness concerns in a letter to the Immigration Division.
propositions.quote: After an off-the-record discussion between counsel and the ID Member at the end of the hearing, the Applicant’s counsel raised procedural fairness concerns in a letter to the ID sent the next day.

propositions.text: The ID could not find non-compliance with paragraph 51(b) because the report only cited paragraph 40(1)(a) and the Minister abandoned paragraph 51(b) allegations.
propositions.quote: She claimed that the ID could not find that the Applicant had not respected paragraph 51(b) of the Regulations because the subsection 44(1) report only cited paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA and the Minister’s counsel had abandoned allegations of inadmissibility for failing to comply with paragraph 51(b) of the Regulations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant’s counsel raised procedural fairness concerns about the ID’s findings and abandoned allegations.

propositions.text: The ID ordered brief submissions on the procedural fairness concern on October 16, 2018.
propositions.quote: Given this concern, the ID ordered that brief submissions be made on this matter on October 16, 2018.

propositions.text: After submissions, the ID orally decided the Applicant was inadmissible for misrepresentation under paragraph 40(1)(a) and issued the Exclusion Order the same day.
propositions.quote: After giving the parties an opportunity to address the concerns raised by the Applicant’s counsel, the ID then rendered its decision orally. It concluded that the Applicant, a foreign national, was inadmissible for misrepresentation under paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA. The ID issued the Exclusion Order on the same day.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the ID ordered submissions, then orally found inadmissibility for misrepresentation and issued the Exclusion Order on October 16, 2018.

propositions.text: The Applicant appealed the ID’s decision to the Immigration Appeal Division, contesting the Exclusion Order’s legality and seeking humanitarian and compassionate relief.
propositions.quote: The Applicant appealed the ID’s decision before the IAD, contesting the legality of the Exclusion Order and asking that it be overturned for humanitarian and compassionate considerations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant appealed the ID’s decision to the IAD, contesting legality and seeking relief.

propositions.text: On the hearing day, the Minister’s representative raised a jurisdiction issue under subsection 63(2) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: On the day of the hearing before the IAD, the Minister’s representative raised an issue of jurisdiction pursuant to subsection 63(2) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The IAD proceeded with Applicant’s testimony on humanitarian considerations but requested additional written submissions on jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The IAD proceeded with the Applicant’s testimony in relation to her humanitarian and compassionate considerations but asked the parties to submit additional written submissions on the issue of jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Minister raised jurisdiction issue at IAD hearing; IAD heard testimony but requested further submissions on jurisdiction.

propositions.text: The IAD dismissed the appeal on August 27, 2019, for lack of jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The IAD rendered its decision on August 27, 2019, and dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

propositions.text: The IAD found no right of appeal under subsection 63(2) because the Applicant’s visa had expired before the Exclusion Order was issued.
propositions.quote: The IAD found that the Applicant did not have a right of appeal pursuant to subsection 63(2) of the IRPA since her permanent resident visa had expired on September 16, 2018, and was no longer valid when the Exclusion Order was issued.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the IAD dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because the Applicant’s visa expired before the Exclusion Order.

propositions.text: Applicant raises two issues in IMM-6268-19: denial of procedural fairness and unreasonableness of the ID’s decision.
propositions.quote: The Applicant raises the following two (2) issues in IMM-6268-19. First, she submits that she was denied procedural fairness and natural justice. By pursuing provisions of the IRPA and the Regulations, and relying on case law not advanced by the Respondent, the ID Member was not impartial and the Applicant was not aware of the case to meet. Second, she submits that the ID’s decision is unreasonable as it was unable to point to any section of the IRPA or the Regulations that specified when the change in marital status had to be disclosed.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues denial of procedural fairness and unreasonableness of the ID’s decision in IMM-6268-19.

propositions.text: Applicant argues the IAD erred in finding no jurisdiction because a valid visa is not invalidated by changed circumstances after issuance.
propositions.quote: In IMM-6270-19, the Applicant argues that the IAD erred in deciding that it did not have jurisdiction to hear the appeal. She argues that “a validly issued visa is not invalidated merely by a change in the circumstances in respect of which it was issued occurring after its issue”.

propositions.text: Applicant argues no statutory authority requires a visa to be unexpired before an Exclusion Order is issued.
propositions.quote: In addition, there is no statutory authority indicating that a visa must not have expired prior to the issuance of the Exclusion Order.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the IAD erred on jurisdiction, claiming a valid visa is not invalidated by changed circumstances and no statute requires unexpired visa.

propositions.text: Vavilov establishes reasonableness as the presumptive standard of review for administrative decisions.
propositions.quote: In Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov], the Supreme Court of Canada held that reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review for decisions made by administrative decision makers (Vavilov at paras 10, 16-17).

propositions.text: No exceptions to reasonableness standard apply here; IAD’s decision is interpretation of its home statute.
propositions.quote: In my view, none of the exceptions described in Vavilov apply here. Contrary to the Applicant’s argument, the IAD’s decision is not a question “regarding the jurisdictional boundaries between two administrative bodies” (Vavilov at para 53). Rather, it is the IAD interpreting subsection 63(2) of the IRPA, its home statute.

propositions.text: Presumption of reasonableness applies to decision maker’s interpretation of enabling statute.
propositions.quote: It is well established that the presumption of reasonableness applies to a decision maker’s interpretation of its enabling statute (Vavilov at para 25; Momi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FCA 163 at para 21).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Vavilov sets reasonableness as standard of review; no exceptions apply; presumption applies to IAD’s statutory interpretation.

propositions.text: Under reasonableness review, court examines decision’s reasoning and outcome for justification, transparency, intelligibility.
propositions.quote: When reviewing a decision under the reasonableness standard, the Court shall examine “the decision actually made by the decision maker, including both the decision maker’s reasoning process and the outcome” (Vavilov at para 83). It must ask itself “whether the decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness — justification, transparency and intelligibility — and whether it is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on the decision” (Vavilov at para 99).

propositions.text: The burden is on the party challenging the decision to show unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the party challenging the decision to show that it is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness review examines decision’s reasoning and outcome; burden on challenger to prove unreasonableness.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issues are assessed on fairness of proceedings, not standard of review.
propositions.quote: With respect to the issue of procedural fairness, the Federal Court of Appeal clarified in Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 [Canadian Pacific] that issues of procedural fairness do not necessarily lend themselves to a standard of review analysis. Rather, the role of this Court is to determine whether the proceedings were fair in all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific at paras 54-56; Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196 at para 35).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness is assessed by fairness of proceedings, not by standard of review.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges denial of procedural fairness because ID pursued paragraph 51(b) despite Respondent abandoning it.
propositions.quote: The Applicant alleges that she was denied procedural fairness because the ID Member pursued the allegations of non-compliance with paragraph 51(b) of the Regulations even though the Respondent had made clear, at the outset of the hearing, its intention to only pursue allegations of inadmissibility under paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges ID Member acted as co-counsel to Respondent and cited case law and provisions not advanced by Respondent, showing bias.
propositions.quote: The ID Member effectively made herself co-counsel to the Respondent and referred in her decision to thirteen (13) Federal Court decisions and sections of the IRPA and the Regulations, which were not advanced by the Respondent. In supplementing the Respondent’s case, the ID Member demonstrated bias.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges breach of procedural fairness because ID indicated she could appeal to IAD.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the ID breached procedural fairness when it indicated to the Applicant that she would be able to appeal its decision to the IAD.

propositions.text: Applicant claims a higher degree of procedural fairness was required due to severe consequences of misrepresentation finding.
propositions.quote: Given the severe consequences that flow from a finding of misrepresentation, the Applicant was entitled to a higher degree of procedural fairness (Likhi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 171 at paras 26-27).

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges denial of procedural fairness due to ID pursuing abandoned allegations, bias, misleading appeal rights, and need for higher fairness.

propositions.text: The Applicant’s procedural fairness argument is without merit.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s argument is without merit.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Applicant’s procedural fairness argument as without merit.

propositions.text: The ID did not pursue allegations under paragraph 51(b) but based the hearing on paragraph 40(1)(a) for misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: Contrary to the Applicant’s assertion, the ID did not pursue the allegations of non-compliance with paragraph 51(b) of the Regulations. The hearing was based on paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA for misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the ID based the hearing on paragraph 40(1)(a) for misrepresentation, not on paragraph 51(b) allegations as the Applicant asserted.

propositions.text: The ID noted the Applicant was a foreign national without unqualified right to enter or remain in Canada.
propositions.quote: the ID first noted that the Applicant was a foreign national who did not have an unqualified right to enter or remain in Canada.

propositions.text: The ID noted a visa applicant has a positive duty of candour under subsections 16(1), 18(1) IRPA and section 51 of the Regulations.
propositions.quote: there was an established principle that a visa applicant seeking to enter Canada has a positive duty of candour, as found in subsections 16(1) and 18(1) of the IRPA and section 51 of the Regulations.

propositions.text: These provisions apply equally to interpreting paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: All are equally applicable to the interpretation of paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The July subsection 44(1) report did not mention section 51 but its allegations pointed to its application.
propositions.quote: While the July subsection 44(1) report did not refer to section 51 of the Regulations, the allegations in the report nevertheless clearly pointed to the application of this provision.

paragraphs.summary: The ID found the Applicant lacked unqualified entry rights, had a duty of candour under IRPA and Regulations, and the report pointed to section 51's application.

propositions.text: The ID found the Applicant had a duty to inform the visa post of her marriage from February 2018 onward.
propositions.quote: It found that when the Applicant married in February 2018, a change in her personal circumstances occurred and from that point on, she had the obligation to inform the visa post.

propositions.text: By withholding marriage information and not correcting visa post records, the Applicant engaged in misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: By withholding the information about her marriage and not correcting the information held by the visa post, the Applicant engaged in misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: The ID found the Applicant had to inform the visa post of her marriage and that withholding this was misrepresentation.

propositions.text: The ID found the Applicant could not establish accompanying dependant status at port of entry due to marital status.
propositions.quote: the ID again referred to section 51 of the Regulations and found that when she presented herself at the port of entry, she could not establish that she was an accompanying dependant given her marital status.

paragraphs.summary: The ID found the Applicant could not prove accompanying dependant status at entry due to her marriage.

propositions.text: Withholding marriage fact was relevant and induced an error in IRPA administration.
propositions.quote: withholding the fact that she had gotten married and was therefore no longer eligible as a dependant child was a relevant matter, which induced an error in the administration of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The ID concluded withholding marriage was relevant and caused an error in IRPA administration.

propositions.text: The ID stated references to section 51 were not to address a separate inadmissibility ground.
propositions.quote: The ID explicitly indicated in its reasons that its references to section 51 of the Regulations were not intended to address a separate ground of inadmissibility.

paragraphs.summary: The ID clarified its references to section 51 were not for a separate inadmissibility ground.

propositions.text: The Applicant knew the case to meet; the July report set out allegations clearly.
propositions.quote: The Applicant cannot reasonably claim that she did not know the case she had to meet. The July subsection 44(1) report clearly sets out the allegations against the Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant did not inform authorities of marital status change before arrival, inducing IRPA error.
propositions.quote: She did not inform the Canadian authorities responsible for processing her application for permanent residence that her marital status had changed prior to her arrival in Canada, thereby inducing an error in the administration of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Had she advised visa post, her visa likely would have been cancelled as no longer eligible as dependant child.
propositions.quote: Had she advised the visa post of her change of marital status prior to her arrival, her visa would likely have been cancelled as she was no longer eligible to land as a dependant child.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant knew the allegations, failed to inform authorities of marriage before arrival, likely causing visa cancellation.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to prove ID Member bias from references to case law and statutes.
propositions.quote: the Applicant has not persuaded me that referring to case law and statutory provisions on issues known to the Applicant demonstrates bias.

propositions.text: ID gave Applicant opportunity to make submissions on relevant legislative provisions before second sitting.
propositions.quote: the ID expressly provided the opportunity to the Applicant, by its direction issued twelve (12) days before the second sitting, to make submissions on the legislative provisions and statutory obligations relevant to her case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no bias by the ID and notes the Applicant had opportunity to make submissions on relevant laws.

propositions.text: Applicant cannot claim procedural fairness breach from ID's erroneous appeal right mention.
propositions.quote: the Applicant cannot claim a breach of procedural fairness or natural justice because the ID erroneously mentioned at the hearing that she had a right of appeal to the IAD.

propositions.text: ID's role was limited to inadmissibility on misrepresentation, not appeal rights.
propositions.quote: The ID’s role was limited to determining whether the Applicant was inadmissible on the grounds of misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Court not persuaded ID's conclusion relied on belief Applicant would appeal to raise humanitarian considerations.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the ID’s conclusion was premised on the belief that the Applicant would be appealing the Exclusion Order so that she could raise humanitarian and compassionate considerations on appeal.

propositions.text: Applicant was represented by counsel; appeal rights come from statute, not ID statements.
propositions.quote: the Applicant was represented by counsel at the hearing and the right of appeal is conferred by statutory authority, not by a statement made by the ID.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no procedural fairness breach from ID's appeal mention; appeal rights are statutory and Applicant had counsel.

propositions.text: Applicant has not shown the ID breached procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: To conclude on this issue, the Applicant has not demonstrated that the ID breached procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Applicant did not demonstrate procedural fairness breach by the ID.

propositions.text: The ID's decision was unreasonable for lacking specific IRPA or Regulation section on timing of marital status disclosure.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the ID’s decision was unreasonable as it was unable to point to any section of the IRPA or the Regulations that specified when the change in marital status had to be disclosed.

propositions.text: The ID relied on a letter sent to Applicant's father with visa as legal grounds for disclosure obligation.
propositions.quote: Instead, it relied on a letter sent to the Applicant’s father with her visa as legal grounds that there was an obligation to disclose this information to the visa office prior to arrival.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the ID's decision was unreasonable for lacking specific legal timing and relying on a letter to her father.

propositions.text: Applicant was candid at port of entry, volunteering marriage info and marriage certificate.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also points to the fact that she was candid at the port of entry regarding her change in marital status. She volunteered this information and provided the marriage certificate.

propositions.text: Applicant questions how withholding info can be rationalized given her candidness at entry.
propositions.quote: Given this fact, the Applicant asks how it can be rationalized that she withheld information.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues she was candid at entry and questions how withholding information is rationalized.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded by the Applicant's arguments.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by these arguments.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not persuaded by the Applicant's arguments.

propositions.text: The ID found Applicant withheld material info inducing IRPA error by not advising visa post before coming to Canada.
propositions.quote: The ID reasonably found that by failing to advise the visa post of her marriage prior to coming to Canada, the Applicant “cut off its ability to review her application”.

propositions.text: Applicant deprived authorities of info leading to further investigation of eligibility.
propositions.quote: She deprived the authorities of information that would have led to further investigation, including the examination into whether she and her dependant – her spouse – met the requirements of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Misrepresentation is not limited to a point in time; correction before final assessment does not make withholding immaterial.
propositions.quote: The ID noted that a misrepresentation is not limited to a particular point in time in the processing of an application and a correction before the final assessment, does not make the withholding of information immaterial.

paragraphs.summary: The ID found the Applicant withheld material info before arrival, depriving authorities and misrepresentation is not time-limited.

propositions.text: Applicant's failure to report marriage was inconsistent with COPR instructions requiring notification before leaving for Canada.
propositions.quote: The ID also found that the Applicant’s failure to report her marriage was inconsistent with the clear instructions communicated in the Confirmation of Permanent Residence [COPR]. The Applicant and her father were required to inform the visa post of any change in marital status or in family composition before they left for Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The ID found the Applicant's failure to report marriage contradicted COPR instructions to notify visa post before departure.

propositions.text: The ID rejected excuse that Applicant was minor and unaware of disclosure obligations, noting she was 20 at marriage.
propositions.quote: The ID rejected the Applicant’s argument that her misrepresentation should be excused on the ground that she was a minor and was unaware of her disclosure obligations. Noting that she was twenty (20) years old when she got married, the ID opined that the Applicant should have been more engaged in the process of her permanent residence application.

paragraphs.summary: The ID rejected the Applicant's minor excuse, noting she was 20 and should have been more engaged.

propositions.text: The ID found unpersuasive Applicant's explanation that marriage was nobody's business; relevance is not applicant's decision.
propositions.quote: The ID also found unpersuasive the Applicant’s explanation that she did not inform the visa post of her marriage because she did not think her marriage was anybody’s business. The ID reasonably noted that it was not for an applicant to decide what is relevant (Singh v Canada, 2015 FC 377 at para 32).

paragraphs.summary: The ID found the Applicant's explanation unpersuasive and noted relevance is not for applicant to decide.

propositions.text: The ID was not required to identify specific statutory provision on timing of disclosure.
propositions.quote: The ID was not required, in my view, to identify a specific statutory provision that indicates at what point in the processing of her application for permanent residence the Applicant had to communicate her change in circumstances.

propositions.text: The ID reasonably concluded failure to report marriage was inconsistent with COPR instructions and duty of candour under IRPA and Regulations.
propositions.quote: It could reasonably conclude that the Applicant’s failure to report her marriage to the visa post was inconsistent not only with the clear instructions identified in the COPR, but also with the general and broad continuing duty of candour required of all applicants under the IRPA and the Regulations to disclose all facts which may be material to their applications for permanent residence

propositions.text: Duty of candour requires disclosure of all material facts under IRPA and Regulations (Kazzi, Dong, Cao).
propositions.quote: (Kazzi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 153 at para 38; Dong v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1108 at para 54; Cao v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 450 at para 28 [Cao]).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the ID reasonably concluded failure to report marriage breached COPR instructions and duty of candour under IRPA and Regulations.

propositions.text: Subsequent disclosure upon arrival does not bar application of paragraph 40(1)(a) IRPA.
propositions.quote: While the Applicant eventually did disclose the information upon her arrival in Canada, the subsequent communication of information does not normally act as a bar to the application of paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA

propositions.text: Paragraph 40(1)(a) applies broadly to misrepresentations even without applicant's knowledge (Tan Gatue, Cao).
propositions.quote: (Tan Gatue v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 730 at paras 23, 25; Cao at para 34).

propositions.text: Disclosure ensures visa officers know all material facts to determine admissibility.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the disclosure is to ensure that visa officers are made aware of all material facts in considering an application in order to determine whether an applicant is admissible to Canada as a permanent resident.

propositions.text: If disclosed before arrival, visa likely cancelled as Applicant no longer eligible as dependant.
propositions.quote: If the Applicant had disclosed her marital status prior to arriving in Canada, the visa officer would have likely cancelled her permanent resident visa, as she could no longer be considered a dependant of her father.

propositions.text: Applicant cannot benefit from being in Canada to circumvent failure to disclose material fact.
propositions.quote: The Applicant cannot take advantage of the fact that she is now in Canada to circumvent her failure to disclose a material fact.

propositions.text: Accepting Applicant's reasoning would encourage withholding info to rectify applications after arrival.
propositions.quote: To accept the Applicant’s reasoning would encourage applicants to withhold information from the visa officers in the hopes of not having their applications rejected prior to coming to Canada and with the intention of being able to rectify their applications once in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that late disclosure does not bar misrepresentation application and accepting Applicant's reasoning would encourage withholding information.

propositions.text: Paragraph 40(1)(a) broadly includes misrepresentations made without applicant's knowledge (Jiang, Cao, Wang).
propositions.quote: Moreover, it is well established that paragraph 40(1)(a) is broadly worded and includes misrepresentations that are made even without the knowledge of the applicant (Jiang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 942 at para 35; Cao at para 31 Wang v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 1059 at paras 55-56).

propositions.text: Exception for honest belief of no withholding is narrow; Applicant not within exception.
propositions.quote: While an exception arises where an applicant can show they honestly believed they were not withholding material information, such exception is narrow. The Applicant has not persuaded me that she falls within the ambit of such an exception.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes paragraph 40(1)(a) covers misrepresentations even without knowledge; exception is narrow and Applicant does not qualify.

propositions.text: The ID could reasonably conclude the Applicant did not fulfill her duty of candour.
propositions.quote: I find that the ID could reasonably conclude that the Applicant did not fulfill her duty of candour.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the ID reasonably concluded the Applicant did not fulfill her duty of candour.

propositions.text: The ID’s decision meets the reasonableness standard and did not breach procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the ID’s decision meets the reasonableness standard set out in Vavilov and that the Applicant’s rights to procedural fairness were not breached.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the ID’s decision is reasonable and procedural fairness was not breached.

propositions.text: Whether the IAD had jurisdiction to hear the appeal given visa expiry and Exclusion Order dates.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue for the IAD was whether it had jurisdiction to hear the appeal, given that the Applicant’s visa expired on September 16, 2018, and that the Exclusion Order was issued on October 16, 2018.

propositions.text: IAD noted four exceptions to visa validity; third exception (visa expires) applied to Applicant.
propositions.quote: Relying on Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Hundal... It found that the third exception, which provides that a visa ceases to be valid when it expires, applied to the Applicant’s case.

paragraphs.summary: The IAD considered its jurisdiction given visa expiry and Exclusion Order, applying the third exception that visa ceases when expired.

propositions.text: Applicant argued visa was still valid when referrals under subsection 44(2) IRPA were issued.
propositions.quote: The IAD then responded to the Applicant’s argument that notwithstanding the third exception, her visa was still valid when the referrals under subsection 44(2) of the IRPA were issued.

propositions.text: IAD referred to Ismail decision that right of appeal requires valid visa when exclusion report issued.
propositions.quote: It referred to the decision in Ismail... where the Court had found that subsection 63(2) of the IRPA granted a right of appeal only to a person who holds a valid permanent resident visa at the time the “exclusion report” is issued.

paragraphs.summary: The IAD addressed Applicant's argument and cited Ismail that appeal rights require valid visa when exclusion report is issued.

propositions.text: IAD found Applicant’s failure to declare change caused delays, not unfair actions by Respondent.
propositions.quote: The IAD found that the cause... was the Applicant’s failure to declare her change in circumstances and to meet the conditions of her visa... not any unfair actions or delays on the part of the Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The IAD found delays were due to Applicant’s failure to declare changes, not Respondent’s unfair actions.

propositions.text: Applicant argued McLeod supports that visa remains valid despite change in circumstances after issue.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the IAD should have relied upon... McLeod... which concluded that “a validly issued visa was not invalidated merely by a change in the circumstances in respect of which it was issued occurring after its issue”.

propositions.text: Applicant argued her visa remained valid at port of entry and when referrals under section 44 IRPA issued.
propositions.quote: She argues that her change in marital status did not invalidate her visa and it remained valid when she presented herself at the port of entry and when the “reports”... were issued.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues McLeod supports her visa remained valid despite change in marital status and at time of referrals.

propositions.text: Applicant’s reliance on McLeod is unfounded.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s reliance on McLeod is unfounded.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Applicant’s reliance on McLeod as unfounded.

propositions.text: McLeod concerned right of appeal under former Immigration Act paragraph 70(2)(b).
propositions.quote: In McLeod, the right of appeal in question was based on paragraph 70(2)(b) of the former Immigration Act...

propositions.text: Under that provision, right of appeal existed if appellant held valid immigrant visa when report was made by immigration officer.
propositions.quote: Under this provision, there was a right of appeal... if the appellant... was in possession of a valid immigrant visa.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains McLeod involved a different statute and right of appeal requiring valid visa when report was made.

propositions.text: Applicant’s right of appeal governed by subsection 63(2) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: In the case at hand, the Applicant’s right of appeal is governed by subsection 63(2) of the IRPA...

propositions.text: Subsection 63(2) IRPA allows appeal by foreign national holding permanent resident visa against removal order under subsection 44(2) or admissibility hearing.
propositions.quote: Right to appeal — visa and removal order... A foreign national who holds a permanent resident visa may appeal...

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant’s appeal right is under subsection 63(2) IRPA allowing appeal if holding valid permanent resident visa.

propositions.text: Subsection 63(2) triggers appeal by issuance of removal order, timing varies by Minister or ID decision.
propositions.quote: The wording of subsection 63(2) of the IRPA establishes that the act that triggers the appeal to the IAD is the issuance of a removal order.

propositions.text: In Applicant’s case, Exclusion Order was made at admissibility hearing.
propositions.quote: In the Applicant’s case, the Exclusion Order was made at the admissibility hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appeal triggers on removal order issuance; here, the Exclusion Order was at admissibility hearing.

propositions.text: Applicant argues IAD misinterpreted Ismail; visa was valid when exclusion reports issued before expiry.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the IAD misinterpreted Ismail... since the “exclusion reports”... were issued... before her visa expired... the IAD should have concluded that she held a valid visa.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the IAD misinterpreted Ismail and her visa was valid when exclusion reports were issued.

propositions.text: Applicant’s interpretation of Ismail is inaccurate; visa validity must be assessed at exclusion order issuance.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the Applicant’s interpretation of Ismail is accurate... for the applicant to have a right of appeal... their visa must be valid when the exclusion order is issued.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant’s interpretation of Ismail inaccurate; visa must be valid when exclusion order is issued.

propositions.text: Subsection 63(2) IRPA applies only to one who currently holds a permanent resident visa, not past holders.
propositions.quote: Subsection 63(2) of the IRPA only applies to one “who holds” a permanent resident visa... having once held a permanent resident visa does not place an applicant within the ambit of this provision.

propositions.text: IAD could reasonably conclude no jurisdiction as Applicant’s visa expired before Exclusion Order.
propositions.quote: The IAD could reasonably conclude that it did not have jurisdiction to hear the appeal given that the Applicant’s visa had expired... and that the Exclusion Order was made...

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 63(2) applies only to current visa holders; the IAD reasonably found no jurisdiction as visa expired.

propositions.text: Applicant seeks costs on a solicitor-client basis in further memorandums.
propositions.quote: In her further memorandums, the Applicant is seeking costs on a solicitor-client basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant seeks solicitor-client costs in further memorandums.

propositions.text: Costs are not awarded on judicial review applications except for special reasons under section 22 of Federal Courts Rules.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 22 of the Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules... costs shall not be awarded on an application for judicial review, except where there are special reasons for doing so.

paragraphs.summary: The court states costs are generally not awarded on judicial review except for special reasons under section 22 rules.

propositions.text: Applicant has not shown special reasons to depart from general rule on costs.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has neither articulated nor demonstrated any special reasons for departing from the general rule.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant has not demonstrated special reasons to award costs.

propositions.text: Applicant requests certification of two questions regarding disclosure obligation and visa validity timing.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has asked the Court to certify two (2) questions: IMM-6268-19... IMM-6270-19...

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant requests certification of two questions about disclosure obligation and visa validity timing.

propositions.text: Respondent opposes certification as questions do not meet certification test.
propositions.quote: The Respondent opposes certification on the ground that the proposed questions do not meet the test for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent opposes certification, arguing the questions fail the certification test.

propositions.text: Certification requires serious, dispositive, broadly significant questions arising from the case, not fact-specific or reference questions.
propositions.quote: The criteria for certification are well established... A question in the nature of a reference or whose answer turns on the unique facts of the case cannot ground a properly certified question...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains certification requires serious, dispositive, broadly significant questions arising from the case.

propositions.text: The first proposed question fails certification as it is fact-specific, not dispositive, and based on incorrect premise.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the question proposed by the Applicant in IMM-6268-19 does not meet the test for certification. It is based on the incorrect premise...

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the first proposed question fails certification for being fact-specific and based on incorrect premise.

propositions.text: The issue of when visa validity is assessed for IAD appeal jurisdiction raises an important question beyond the parties' interests and is determinative of an appeal
propositions.quote: I find that the issue of when the validity of the visa must be assessed for the purpose of the right of appeal to the IAD provided by subsection 63(2) of the IRPA raises an important question that transcends the interests of the parties in this case and would be determinative of an appeal.

propositions.text: The proposed question is rephrased and certified as a question of general importance regarding when visa validity is assessed for IAD jurisdiction under subsection 63(2) IRPA
propositions.quote: I would, however, rephrase the proposed question and certify the following: For the purposes of determining its jurisdiction to hear an appeal pursuant to subsection 63(2) of the IRPA, shall the validity of the permanent resident visa be assessed by the IAD at the time of arrival in Canada, at the time the report under subsection 44(1) is made, at the time it is referred to the ID, as the case may be, or at the time the exclusion order is issued?

propositions.text: Applications for judicial review are dismissed; no costs awarded; no question certified in IMM-6268-19; question certified in IMM-6270-19 as stated
propositions.quote: The applications for judicial review are dismissed; No costs are awarded; No question of general importance is certified in IMM-6268-19; The following question of general importance is certified in IMM 6270-19: For the purposes of determining its jurisdiction to hear an appeal pursuant to subsection 63(2) of the IRPA, shall the validity of the permanent resident visa be assessed by the IAD at the time of arrival in Canada, at the time the report under subsection 44(1) is made, at the time it is referred to the ID, as the case may be, or at the time the exclusion order is issued?

propositions.text: Judgment and reasons dated April 21, 2021, by Judge Sylvie E. Roussel, with appearances and solicitors noted
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT in IMM-6268-19 and IMM-6270-19 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: ... “Sylvie E. Roussel” Judge FEDERAL COURT ... JUDGMENT AND REASONS: ROUSSEL J. DATED: APRIL 21, 2021 APPEARANCES: Mary Lam For The Applicant Asha Gafar For The Respondent SOLICITORS OF RECORD: Mary Lam Barrister & Solicitor Toronto, Ontario For The Applicant Attorney General of Canada Toronto, Ontario For The Respondent

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa validity timing issue important and certifies a rephrased question for IMM-6270-19; dismisses reviews; records judgment details.
